chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Umayyah (Isa), from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever preserves his omission and completes it, then there is no Sajdat al-Sahw (two prostrations of forgetfulness) upon him. For the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) prayed Dhuhr with the people for two Rak'at, then he was forgetful and gave Salam. So Dhul-Shimalayn said to him, 'O Messenger of Allah, has anything been revealed regarding the Salat?' He said, 'And what is that?' He said, 'You only prayed two Rak'at.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Are you saying the like of his words?' They said, 'Yes'. So he (peace be upon him and his family) stood up and completed the Salat with them and prostrated with them the two prostrations of forgetfulness.'

He (the narrator) said, 'I said, 'What is your view of the one who prays two Rak'at and thinks that they are four, so he gives Salam and departs, then remembers after he has gone that he only prayed two Rak'at?'' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He should restart the Salat from its beginning.'

He (the narrator) said, 'I said, 'So what was the matter that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did not restart the Salat, but rather he completed with them what remained of his Salat?'' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did not leave his seat. So if he had not left his seat, then let him complete what was deficient from his Salat, when he had preserved the first two Rak'at.'

key_terms.ذُو الشِّمَالَيْنِ: A companion of the Prophet, known as 'Possessor of the Two Lefts'

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for Sajdat al-Sahw if one realizes a mistake after leaving the prayer spot?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi distinguishes between minor forgetfulness (sahw) where the worshipper remains in the prayer spot, requiring only two compensatory prostrations, and major error where departure necessitates restarting the prayer entirely. Shia jurists emphasize this distinction to highlight the Prophet’s practical application of ease in worship, contrasting it with stricter views that might require full repetition. The narration underscores the importance of maintaining continuity in ritual acts when possible, reflecting the Shia principle of facilitating religious obligations.
